notes:
I researched Leviticus 23:23–44, but only partly. I ran out of searches and page reads before covering every verse and every tradition. Most notes below come from the Enduring Word page and the BibleHub and StudyLight commentary pages I could read. I left out what I couldn't find, and the gaps are listed at the end.

**vv. 23–25: Feast of Trumpets**

- **v. 23:** Ellicott says this new heading marks Trumpets and Atonement as a separate message from God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/23-23.htm
- **v. 24, the season:** Rooker, quoted by Guzik, says the three fall feasts fell in September/October, during the grape, fig and olive harvests. Guzik says the trumpets called God's people together. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/
- **v. 24, "trumpets":**
  - Barnes says the Hebrew means "shouting" and never actually names trumpets. Still, he accepts the tradition that horns were blown across the land.
  - Poole says the blowing was louder than the usual new-moon blowing and happened in every city, not only Jerusalem. He gives two reasons: to mark the civil new year, and to make the seventh month a kind of "sabbatical month."
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/23-24.htm
- **v. 24, a call to repentance:** Gill reports Jewish teachers who said the trumpet was meant to stir fear and repentance, getting people ready for the Day of Atonement. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-24.html
- **v. 24, who the "memorial" reminds (a real disagreement):**
  - The Expositor's Bible says the reminder came from God to Israel: the King announcing that the holy month had begun. It rejects the idea that Israel was reminding God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/leviticus-23.html
  - Ellicott, by contrast, says the synagogue read it as "reminding" God of the patriarchs. That is why Genesis 21–22 (the binding of Isaac) is read on this day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/23-24.htm
- **v. 24, pointing to Christ:**
  - Matthew Henry says the trumpets stand for gospel preaching, which calls people to repent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/23-24.htm
  - The BibleHub study notes link the trumpet to Christ's return (1 Thessalonians 4:16). https://biblehub.com/leviticus/23-24.htm
- **v. 25:** Ezra read the law publicly on this same day (Nehemiah 8:2). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-25.html

**vv. 26–32: Day of Atonement**

- **v. 27, "humble yourselves":**
  - Guzik notes that neither Leviticus 16:29 nor this verse says exactly what this means. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/
  - Ellicott says it simply means fasting. Benson and Poole add bitter repentance for national sins, especially the golden calf. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/23-27.htm
  - Calvin calls the fast an outward sign of repentance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-27.html
- **v. 28, why no work:** Matthew Henry says getting right with God takes "the whole man" and your full attention, so everything else had to stop. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-27.html
- **v. 29, "cut off":**
  - Guzik notes that no other feast in this chapter carries such a strong penalty. He quotes a source calling it the usual phrase for being expelled from Israel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/
  - Henry says every soul had to humble itself, because everyone was guilty before God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-27.html
- **v. 30, a gospel reading:** Kelly reads the ban on work as teaching that people contribute nothing to atonement; only the Saviour does that work. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-27.html
- **v. 32, evening to evening:** Henry says the fast began on the evening of the ninth day, so people stopped work before sunset. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-27.html

**vv. 33–44: Feast of Tabernacles**

- **v. 34:** Guzik says the feast began on 15 Tishri and lasted seven days plus one extra. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/
- **v. 36, the eighth day:**
  - Guzik cites Maclaren on a Talmud custom: each day a priest drew water from the Pool of Siloam. He connects this to Jesus' cry on "the last day" (John 7:37). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia also identifies the eighth day with the "great day" of John 7:37. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14425a.htm
- **vv. 37–38:** Matthew Henry draws the lesson that special services never excuse us from our regular duties. At least one ordinary Sabbath always fell within the feast. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-33.html
- **v. 39:** The feast began and ended with rest; Guzik calls it a time of refreshment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/
- **v. 40, the branches:**
  - Barnes says the "fruit" is the citron. Each worshipper carried a bundle of branches in one hand and a citron in the other. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/23-40.htm
  - Keil and Delitzsch disagree. They say the branches were for building the booths, and that the hand-held bundle custom "has no foundation in the law" but was borrowed later. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/23-40.htm
  - Coffman takes "fruit" to mean branches for the booths, pointing out that the willow bears no fruit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-40.html
- **v. 40, rejoicing:** Guzik says this is the only one of the seven feasts where rejoicing is commanded. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/
- **vv. 42–43, the booths:**
  - Guzik notes that in the wilderness Israel lived this way all the time, because they had to. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/
  - Henry says many think Jesus was born around this feast and "tabernacled among us" (John 1:14). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-33.html
  - Clarke gives the feast's first purpose as keeping alive the memory of God's care in bringing Israel out of Egypt and through the wilderness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/leviticus-23.html
- **Trumpets to Tabernacles as one sequence:** Matthew Henry says the fasting of Atonement got people ready for the joy of Tabernacles. "Those that sow in tears shall reap in joy." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_023.cfm

**Where Christian readings differ: what the fall feasts point to**

I couldn't find sources from named Protestant traditions disagreeing over these verses. The real dividing line I found is between future-prophecy readings and gospel readings.

- **Future prophecy:**
  - Guzik (Enduringword) reads Trumpets as the rapture, Atonement as Israel's salvation in the Great Tribulation, and Tabernacles as the millennium. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-23/
  - Constable likewise ties Atonement to Christ's second coming and Israel's repentance. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-27.html
- **Gospel and church age:** Matthew Henry reads the sequence as gospel preaching, then Christ's atonement, then believers living as pilgrims (see the Trumpets notes above).
- **Church age:** Coffman cites scholars who see the long gap between Pentecost and Trumpets as the age of the Church. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/leviticus-23.html

**Other views**

- **Catholic:**
  - Haydock links the trumpets to the Sinai thunder and the coming fast. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/23-24.html
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia says Jews kept Tabernacles mainly to remember the wilderness tents and give thanks for the Promised Land. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/14425a.htm
- **Older critical observations:** Clarke mentions Plutarch's idea that the feast was Bacchus worship. Clarke also thinks Trumpets may simply have marked the new year. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/leviticus-23.html

**Not found:**
- Notes from bibleodyssey.org and netbible.org
- Orthodox readings (oca.org)
- Prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on these verses
- Sources from Lutheran, Methodist, Pentecostal or Baptist teachers specifically
- Specific comment on vv. 26, 31, 35, 41 and 44
